nameStory: This jelly fungus gets its "fan-shaped" name from its distinctive spoon or spatula-like appearance that flares out like a tiny hand fan. The scientific name "spathularia" comes from the Latin word for spoon or spatula, perfectly describing these elegant, flattened fruiting bodies that emerge from decaying wood.
description: Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus is a small, translucent fungus that looks like tiny amber or orange spoons growing from dead wood. These gelatinous organisms have a unique rubbery texture and can range from pale yellow to bright orange in color. Individual specimens are typically small, often less than an inch across, but they frequently grow in clusters that can cover several inches of a log or branch. Like other jelly fungi, they can shrivel up during dry weather and plump back up when moisture returns.

idTips.label: Spoon Shape
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive flattened, fan-like or spoon-shaped fruiting bodies that are wider at the top than the base, feeling rubbery and gelatinous to the touch

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Ranges from pale translucent yellow to bright orange, often with a glossy, wet appearance even when dry

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels like firm jelly or rubber when fresh, can be gently squeezed without breaking, and bounces back to shape

idTips.label: Growing Pattern
idTips.description: Often grows in small clusters or groups on the same piece of wood, with individual specimens seeming to emerge directly from the bark surface

idTips.label: Wood Preference
idTips.description: Always found on dead hardwood branches and logs, never on living trees or on the ground

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual specimens are quite small, typically less than an inch wide, but noticeable due to their bright color and unusual shape

habitat: Look for Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus on dead branches and fallen logs of hardwood trees throughout New England's forests. They particularly favor oak, maple, and birch wood that's been dead for some time but hasn't completely decomposed. You'll often find them in mixed deciduous forests, along woodland edges, and sometimes in parks where dead wood is left to decompose naturally.

seasonality.spring: Fresh specimens begin appearing on dead wood as temperatures warm and spring rains provide consistent moisture. Look for bright, plump fruiting bodies that have recovered from winter's dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when specimens are most abundant and colorful, though they may shrivel during hot, dry spells and plump up again after rain showers.
seasonality.fall: Still active and producing new fruiting bodies, especially during wet autumn weather. The orange specimens can be particularly striking against colorful fall foliage.
seasonality.winter: May persist in shriveled form during mild winters, becoming dormant but not dead, ready to rehydrate when conditions improve in spring.

funFact: This little fungus is actually edible and commercially cultivated in some parts of the world as a food additive, prized for its unique gelatinous texture that can add body to soups and sauces - imagine finding gourmet ingredients right on your local hiking trail!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Orange Jelly Spot, which forms rounded, cushion-like blobs rather than the distinctive spoon shapes. Remember: if it looks like a tiny orange spatula or fan, it's likely Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus; if it's a formless orange blob, it's probably Orange Jelly Spot.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "jelly fungus," these organisms are quite different from the jellyfish-like fungi many people think of. The jelly fungi belong to their own special group and have a unique ability to dry up completely during drought and then rehydrate when moisture returns, almost like natural sponges.
compareHints: Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus stands out from its relatives Orange Jelly Spot and Yellow Hat Jelly by its distinctive flattened, spoon-like shape. While Orange Jelly Spot forms irregular cushions or blobs and Yellow Hat Jelly creates small button or cap-like structures, Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus maintains its characteristic spatula form. The fan shape is so distinctive that once you've seen it, you'll easily distinguish it from other orange jelly fungi.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange Jelly Spot forms simple, rounded cushions while its relative Fan-shaped Jelly Fungus grows in distinctive spoon or fan shapes with flattened tops.
